title: Articles & gender
summary: How to choose il/lo/l'/la and un/uno/una/un', and how a noun's ending tells you its gender.

sections.heading: Definite articles
sections.body: Italian has seven forms of *the*, chosen by the gender and number of the noun and by the first sound of the word that follows. The basic masculine forms are *il* (singular) and *i* (plural); the basic feminine forms are *la* (singular) and *le* (plural). Before a vowel, both *lo* and *la* shorten to *l'* in the singular; in the plural, *gli* is kept whole and *le* is never shortened.
table: Before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, y, i+vowel

examples.it: Il treno per Roma parte alle otto.
examples.en: The train to Rome leaves at eight.

examples.it: Gli studenti aspettano lo psicologo.
examples.en: The students are waiting for the psychologist.

examples.it: L'acqua è fredda, ma le onde sono calme.
examples.en: The water is cold, but the waves are calm.

sections.heading: When to use lo and gli
sections.body: *Lo* (plural *gli*) replaces *il* (plural *i*) before a masculine noun that begins with an *impure s* (s followed by a consonant: *sport, studio, sbaglio*), with *z* (*zaino, zucchero*), with *gn* (*gnocco*), with *ps* or *pn* (*psicologo, pneumatico*), with *x* or *y* (*xilofono, yogurt*), or with *i* followed by a vowel (*iodio, iato*). *Gli* is also the plural before any vowel (*gli amici, gli uomini*). The same rule decides the indefinite article *uno* and the articulated prepositions (*allo, dello, sullo, negli, dagli*).
sections.tip: The rule is about sound, not spelling: *lo sport* but *il sole*, because in *sole* the s is followed by a vowel. In everyday speech *il pneumatico* is also heard and accepted.

sections.heading: Indefinite articles
sections.body: The indefinite article has four written forms. Masculine *un* is used before consonants and vowels alike and never takes an apostrophe (*un amico*). Masculine *uno* follows exactly the same rule as *lo* (*uno studente, uno zio, uno psicologo, uno yogurt*). Feminine *una* becomes *un'* before a vowel (*un'amica, un'ora*), so an apostrophe after *un* always signals a feminine noun.
table: Before s+cons., z, gn, ps, x, y

examples.it: Ho comprato un ombrello e un'agenda.
examples.en: I bought an umbrella and a diary.

examples.it: C'è uno sconosciuto alla porta.
examples.en: There is a stranger at the door.

sections.tip: *Un'amica* (f) but *un amico* (m): the apostrophe is the only visible difference in speech, so remember that *un* is never shortened.

sections.heading: Gender from the ending: -o, -a, -e
sections.body: Most nouns ending in *-o* are masculine (*il libro, il tavolo*) and most nouns ending in *-a* are feminine (*la casa, la sedia*). Nouns ending in *-e* can be either gender and must be learned with their article: *il pane, il fiore, il nome* are masculine, *la notte, la chiave, la carne* are feminine. A few *-o* nouns are feminine (*la mano, la radio, la foto, la moto, l'auto*), mostly because they are shortenings of longer feminine words (*fotografia, motocicletta, automobile*).

examples.it: La mano destra mi fa male.
examples.en: My right hand hurts.

examples.it: Il fiore è sul tavolo accanto alla chiave.
examples.en: The flower is on the table next to the key.

sections.heading: Reliable feminine endings: -tà, -tù, -ione, -trice, -ie
sections.body: Some endings are almost always feminine. Nouns in *-tà* and *-tù* (*la città, la libertà, la virtù*) are feminine and invariable in the plural. Nouns in *-ione* (*la stazione, la lezione, la televisione*) are feminine, as are those in *-trice* (*l'attrice, la scrittrice*) and *-ie* (*la serie, la specie*). Nouns in *-i* are mostly feminine and invariable (*la crisi, l'analisi, la tesi*), though *il brindisi* is masculine.

examples.it: La stazione è vicina all'università.
examples.en: The station is near the university.

examples.it: Questa crisi durerà anni.
examples.en: This crisis will last for years.

sections.heading: Masculine nouns in -a: Greek words, -ista, -ore
sections.body: A group of nouns of Greek origin ending in *-ma* is masculine and forms its plural in *-i*: *il problema / i problemi, il tema, il sistema, il programma, il clima, il dramma, il diploma, il panorama, il teorema*. Other masculine *-a* nouns include *il poeta, il pianeta, il papa, il papà, il cinema, il vaglia*. Nouns in *-ista* (*il/la turista, il/la giornalista, il/la dentista*) and *-cida*, *-iatra* (*l'omicida, il/la pediatra*) have the same form for both genders in the singular; the article tells the gender, and the plural is *-isti* (m) / *-iste* (f). Masculine nouns in *-ore* (*l'attore, il pittore, lo scrittore*) usually have a feminine in *-trice* (*l'attrice, la pittrice, la scrittrice*); *il dottore* has *la dottoressa*, *il professore* has *la professoressa*.

examples.it: Abbiamo un problema con il programma.
examples.en: We have a problem with the programme.

examples.it: La giornalista ha intervistato l'attrice.
examples.en: The journalist interviewed the actress.

sections.tip: If a noun ends in *-ma* and is an abstract or technical word (*problema, sistema, tema, clima, schema*), bet on masculine. Everyday *-ma* nouns like *la mamma, la crema, la lacrima, la fiamma* are feminine.

sections.heading: Foreign words and abbreviations
sections.body: Nouns borrowed from other languages ending in a consonant are usually masculine and invariable: *il computer / i computer, il film, lo sport, il bar, il weekend, l'autobus, lo yogurt*. They take the article the initial sound requires (*lo sport, lo yogurt, l'hotel*). A few are feminine because of the Italian word they replace: *la mail / l'e-mail* (from *la posta*), *la chat*, *la password* (*la parola d'ordine*), *la star*. Abbreviations keep the gender of the full word: *la foto (fotografia), la bici (bicicletta), il cinema (cinematografo), il frigo (frigorifero), la metro (metropolitana)*. Acronyms follow the gender of their main noun: *la TV, la BBC, il PIL, l'ONU (f)*.

examples.it: Ho visto un film al cinema e poi ho preso la metro.
examples.en: I saw a film at the cinema and then took the metro.

examples.it: Ti mando una mail con la password.
examples.en: I'll send you an email with the password.

sections.heading: Using or dropping the article
sections.body: Italian uses the definite article more than English. It appears before general and abstract nouns (*Amo la musica; Il tempo vola*), before languages (*Studio l'italiano*), before possessives (*la mia casa*), before titles when speaking about someone (*Il dottor Rossi è arrivato*), before days of the week to mean *every* (*Il lunedì vado in palestra*), and with time and dates (*Sono le tre; il 5 maggio*). It is dropped before singular family members with a possessive (*mia madre, tuo fratello*, but *la mia mamma, i miei fratelli*), in many fixed expressions with *in* and *a* (*in cucina, a casa, a scuola, in ufficio*), and when addressing someone by title (*Buongiorno, dottor Rossi*).

examples.it: Il sabato mia sorella va sempre in piscina.
examples.en: On Saturdays my sister always goes to the pool.

examples.it: La signora Bianchi parla bene il francese.
examples.en: Mrs Bianchi speaks French well.

examples.it: Buonasera, signora Bianchi!
examples.en: Good evening, Mrs Bianchi!

title: Plurals
summary: Regular plural endings, the spelling rules for -co/-go/-ca/-ga/-cia/-gia/-io, invariable nouns, and the irregular and double plurals you must memorise.

sections.heading: The three regular patterns
sections.body: Italian plurals change the final vowel rather than adding *-s*. Nouns in *-o* take *-i*, nouns in *-a* take *-e*, and nouns in *-e* take *-i* whatever their gender. The article changes with the noun (*il → i, lo/l' → gli, la/l' → le*). Masculine nouns in *-a* (*il problema, il poeta, il turista*) follow the *-e/-i* logic rather than the *-a/-e* one: *i problemi, i poeti, i turisti*.

la casa → le case; la ragazza → le ragazze
il problema → i problemi; il pianista → i pianisti
il fiore → i fiori; la notte → le notti

examples.it: I ragazzi e le ragazze arrivano alle nove.
examples.en: The boys and girls arrive at nine.

examples.it: Le chiavi sono sui tavoli.
examples.en: The keys are on the tables.

sections.heading: -ca / -ga → -che / -ghe
sections.body: Feminine nouns in *-ca* and *-ga* insert an *h* in the plural to keep the hard *k* and *g* sounds: *l'amica → le amiche, la banca → le banche, la riga → le righe, la collega → le colleghe*. Masculine nouns in *-ca* and *-ga* take *-chi* and *-ghi* instead: *il collega → i colleghi, il monarca → i monarchi, lo stratega → gli strateghi*. The same *h* appears in adjectives (*bianca → bianche, lunga → lunghe*).
sections.tip: *Belga* is the one common exception: masculine plural *i belgi*, not *belghi*.

sections.heading: -co / -go: stress decides
sections.body: For masculine nouns in *-co* and *-go*, the general rule depends on where the stress falls. If the stress is on the syllable immediately before the ending (*fuò-co, al-bèr-go*), the plural keeps the hard sound with *h*: *fuochi, alberghi, parchi, giochi, laghi, luoghi*. If the stress falls earlier (*mè-di-co, psi-cò-lo-go*), the plural is *-ci / -gi*: *medici, psicologi, sindaci, biologi*. The most important exceptions are stressed on the penultimate syllable yet still soften: *amico → amici, nemico → nemici, greco → greci, porco → porci*. Words in *-logo* referring to people take *-logi* (*psicologi, biologi*), while things in *-logo* take *-loghi* (*cataloghi, dialoghi, monologhi*).

examples.it: I miei amici sono medici in due alberghi diversi.
examples.en: My friends are doctors at two different hotels.

examples.it: I cataloghi dei parchi sono pronti.
examples.en: The catalogues of the parks are ready.

sections.heading: -cia / -gia: does the i carry stress or follow a vowel?
sections.body: Feminine nouns in *-cia* and *-gia* keep the *i* in the plural when the *i* is stressed (*la farmacìa → le farmacie, la bugìa → le bugie, l'allergìa → le allergie*) or when *-cia/-gia* is preceded by a vowel (*la camicia → le camicie, la valigia → le valigie, la ciliegia → le ciliegie*). When the ending is preceded by a consonant and the *i* is unstressed, the *i* drops: *l'arancia → le arance, la spiaggia → le spiagge, la faccia → le facce, la pioggia → le piogge*. The *i* was only there to soften the *c/g* before *a*, and *-e* is already a soft vowel.

sections.tip: *Valige* and *ciliege* are also seen and accepted, but the vowel-before rule gives the safer exam spelling *valigie, ciliegie*.

sections.heading: -io: one i or two?
sections.body: Masculine nouns in *-io* form the plural with a single *-i* when the *i* is unstressed: *lo studio → gli studi, il figlio → i figli, il viaggio → i viaggi, l'occhio → gli occhi, il negozio → i negozi*. When the *i* is stressed (*zìo, addìo, pendìo, mormorìo*), the plural has two: *gli zii, gli addii, i pendii*. The rare ambiguities that arise (*principi* = princes or principles) are resolved by context or, formally, by an accent (*princìpi* = principles).

sections.heading: Invariable nouns
sections.body: Several groups of nouns do not change in the plural, so only the article shows the number. These are: nouns with a final accented vowel (*la città → le città, il caffè → i caffè, l'università → le università*); nouns ending in a consonant, mostly foreign (*il bar → i bar, lo sport → gli sport, il film → i film*); monosyllables (*il re → i re, la gru → le gru*); nouns in *-i* and *-ie* (*la crisi → le crisi, la serie → le serie*, except *la moglie → le mogli* and *la superficie → le superfici*); abbreviations (*la foto → le foto, il cinema → i cinema, la bici → le bici, l'auto → le auto, la moto → le moto*); and a handful of nouns in *-a* like *il vaglia → i vaglia*.

examples.it: Ho visitato tre città e ho fatto molte foto.
examples.en: I visited three cities and took a lot of photos.

examples.it: I film di quei re sono lunghi.
examples.en: The films about those kings are long.

sections.heading: Irregular plurals
sections.body: A small set of nouns has an irregular plural inherited from Latin. *L'uomo → gli uomini* is the most frequent. *Il dio → gli dei* also takes the unusual article *gli* before a consonant (*gli dei*, not *i dei*). *Il bue → i buoi*, *il tempio → i templi*, *la mano → le mani* (feminine in *-o*, plural *-i*), *l'ala → le ali* and *l'arma → le armi* (feminine in *-a* with plural *-i*), *la moglie → le mogli*, *la superficie → le superfici*.
table: plural article gli before a consonant

examples.it: Gli uomini antichi pregavano molti dei.
examples.en: Ancient men prayed to many gods.

examples.it: Ho le mani fredde e le ali del cappello si sono rotte.
examples.en: My hands are cold and the brim of my hat has broken.

sections.heading: Double plurals: braccio/braccia, uovo/uova
sections.body: Some masculine nouns in *-o*, mostly parts of the body, have a feminine plural in *-a* which is the normal, concrete one (*il braccio → le braccia, il dito → le dita, l'osso → le ossa, il ginocchio → le ginocchia, il labbro → le labbra, il ciglio → le ciglia, l'uovo → le uova, il paio → le paia, il centinaio → le centinaia, il migliaio → le migliaia, il miglio → le miglia, il riso → le risa*). Several also keep a regular masculine plural in *-i* with a different, often figurative or individual, meaning: *i bracci* (arms of a chair, of a river), *i diti* (individual fingers considered one by one), *gli ossi* (bones for a dog), *i muri* (individual walls) vs *le mura* (city walls), *i membri* (members) vs *le membra* (limbs), *i frutti* (results, individual fruits) vs *le frutta* (rare: fruit as food, usually *la frutta*), *i cigli* (edges of a road) vs *le ciglia* (eyelashes).

examples.it: Mi fanno male le braccia e le ginocchia.
examples.en: My arms and knees hurt.

examples.it: Le mura di Lucca sono famose; i muri di casa mia sono bianchi.
examples.en: Lucca's city walls are famous; the walls of my house are white.

examples.it: Ho comprato due paia di scarpe e sei uova.
examples.en: I bought two pairs of shoes and six eggs.

sections.tip: Adjectives agree with the feminine plural: *le braccia lunghe, le uova fresche, le dita sporche*.

sections.heading: Plural-only and singular-only nouns
sections.body: Some nouns exist only in the plural: *gli occhiali* (glasses), *i pantaloni* (trousers), *le forbici* (scissors), *le nozze* (wedding), *le ferie* (holidays from work), *i dintorni* (surroundings), *le stoviglie* (crockery), *i viveri* (provisions), *le posate* (cutlery), *le redini* (reins), *gli spiccioli* (small change). They take plural verbs and plural adjectives (*I pantaloni sono stretti*). Others are normally singular only: mass nouns (*il latte, il pane, la fame, la sete*), abstractions (*il coraggio, la pazienza*) and collective *la gente*, which takes a singular verb (*La gente parla*), unlike English *people*.

examples.it: Dove sono i miei occhiali? Le forbici sono nel cassetto.
examples.en: Where are my glasses? The scissors are in the drawer.

examples.it: La gente è stanca di aspettare.
examples.en: People are tired of waiting.

title: Adjectives
summary: Agreement, invariable colours, where the adjective goes and how position changes meaning, the special forms of bello/quello/buono, and comparatives and superlatives.

sections.heading: Two agreement classes
sections.body: Every adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes. Adjectives in *-o* have four forms (*-o, -a, -i, -e*): *rosso, rossa, rossi, rosse*. Adjectives in *-e* have only two (*-e* singular, *-i* plural) and do not mark gender: *grande, grandi; verde, verdi; felice, felici*. A few adjectives in *-a* (*ottimista, egoista, belga*) behave like *-ista* nouns: *ottimista* for both genders in the singular, *ottimisti / ottimiste* in the plural. When one adjective describes nouns of different genders, it goes masculine plural: *Marco e Anna sono simpatici*.

examples.it: Le case nuove sono grandi e luminose.
examples.en: The new houses are big and bright.

examples.it: I ragazzi sono simpatici; le ragazze sono simpatiche.
examples.en: The boys are nice; the girls are nice.

sections.tip: Feminine adjectives in *-ca/-ga* always take *-che/-ghe* (*simpatiche, larghe*); masculine *-co* follows the stress rule of nouns (*bianchi* but *simpatici*).

sections.heading: Invariable adjectives and colours
sections.body: Colours that come from nouns are invariable: *rosa* (pink), *viola* (purple), *blu* (blue), *beige, lilla, arancione* (often used invariably, though *arancioni* is also heard), *marrone* (*marroni* is accepted). Compound colours are invariable too: *verde scuro, rosso chiaro, giallo limone*. Most colours are ordinary adjectives and agree normally: *rosso, giallo, nero, bianco, verde, grigio, azzurro*. Other invariables include *pari, dispari, perbene, dabbene* and words like *super, extra* used as adjectives.
table: verde scuro, rosso fuoco, grigio perla

examples.it: Ha comprato due maglie blu e una sciarpa rosa.
examples.en: She bought two blue sweaters and a pink scarf.

examples.it: Le pareti sono verde chiaro.
examples.en: The walls are light green.

sections.heading: Position: after the noun by default
sections.body: The neutral position of an Italian adjective is after the noun: *una macchina rossa, un libro interessante*. Adjectives that classify or distinguish (colours, shapes, nationalities, materials, technical or relational adjectives, past participles) must follow: *il vino italiano, la chiesa gotica, un tavolo rotondo, il partito socialista*. Adjectives modified by an adverb also follow (*una casa molto grande*). A small group of very common descriptive adjectives (*bello, brutto, buono, cattivo, grande, piccolo, giovane, vecchio, nuovo, stesso, altro, primo, ultimo*) often goes before the noun when it expresses a subjective or expected quality rather than a contrast. Placing an adjective before the noun makes it feel more emotional or literary; placing it after makes it more precise and restrictive.

examples.it: Abbiamo visto un bel film francese.
examples.en: We saw a lovely French film.

examples.it: È una persona gentile e una brava insegnante.
examples.en: She is a kind person and a good teacher.

examples.it: Preferisco le scarpe nere alle scarpe marroni.
examples.en: I prefer the black shoes to the brown ones.

sections.tip: Possessives, demonstratives, numbers and quantity words (*molto, poco, tanto, troppo, ogni, qualche*) always precede the noun.

sections.heading: Adjectives that change meaning with position
sections.body: With some adjectives the position is not just a matter of style: before the noun they have a figurative or evaluative meaning, after the noun a literal one. *Un grande uomo* is a great man; *un uomo grande* is a big man. *Un povero ragazzo* is an unfortunate boy; *un ragazzo povero* has no money. *Un vecchio amico* is a long-standing friend; *un amico vecchio* is elderly. *Una nuova macchina* is a different car (new to me); *una macchina nuova* is brand new. *Una certa notizia* is some news or other; *una notizia certa* is confirmed.
table: una nuova casa (another, new to me)
un figlio unico (an only child / unique)

examples.it: È un vecchio amico, ma non è un uomo vecchio.
examples.en: He is an old friend, but he is not an old man.

examples.it: Ho comprato diversi vestiti, tutti di colori diversi.
examples.en: I bought several dresses, all in different colours.

sections.heading: Bello and quello follow the definite article
sections.body: When *bello* and *quello* stand before a noun, their endings copy the definite article that the noun would take: *bel / quel* (like *il*), *bei / quei* (like *i*), *bello / quello* (like *lo*), *begli / quegli* (like *gli*), *bell' / quell'* before a vowel in the singular, *bella / quella* (like *la*), *belle / quelle* (like *le*). After the noun, or after *essere*, *bello* is regular: *un ragazzo bello, i film sono belli*. Note *begli* before masculine plural vowels and impure s (*begli occhi, begli studenti*) but *bei* before ordinary consonants (*bei libri*).
table: begli occhi, quegli alberi, quegli studenti

examples.it: Che begli occhi ha quel bambino!
examples.en: What beautiful eyes that child has!

examples.it: Quegli studenti hanno scritto dei bei temi.
examples.en: Those students wrote some nice essays.

sections.tip: As a pronoun (without a noun), *quello* has only four forms: *quello, quella, quelli, quelle* (*Quale vuoi? Quelli.*).

sections.heading: Buono behaves like un / una
sections.body: Before a noun, the singular of *buono* follows the indefinite article. Masculine *buon* (like *un*) is used before consonants and vowels: *un buon libro, un buon amico, buon appetito*. *Buono* (like *uno*) before impure s, z, ps, gn, y: *un buono studente, un buono zaino*. Feminine *buona* before consonants and *buon'* before vowels: *una buona pizza, una buon'idea* (though *buona idea* is now also common). The plurals are regular (*buoni, buone*); *santo* works the same way (*san Pietro, sant'Antonio, santo Stefano, santa Maria, sant'Anna*), and *grande* may shorten to *gran* before a consonant (*un gran piacere, una gran fame*).
table: buon giorno, buon anno, buon appetito

examples.it: Buon viaggio e buona fortuna!
examples.en: Have a good trip and good luck!

examples.it: È un buono studente e un buon amico.
examples.en: He is a good student and a good friend.

sections.heading: Comparatives
sections.body: The comparative of majority uses *più* and the comparative of minority uses *meno*; the comparative of equality uses *(così)… come* or *(tanto)… quanto*. The second term of comparison is introduced by *di* when comparing two nouns or pronouns (*Marco è più alto di Luca; Roma è più grande di Firenze*) and by *che* when comparing two adjectives, two verbs, two adverbs, two quantities, or two nouns preceded by a preposition (*È più bello che utile; È più facile parlare che scrivere; Ci sono più ragazzi che ragazze; Fa più caldo a Roma che a Milano*). Before a number or a clause, use *di* (*più di dieci; più di quanto pensassi*).
table: Anna è più veloce di Marco.
Questo libro è meno noioso di quello.
Mi piace più leggere che guardare la TV.

examples.it: Il treno è più comodo dell'autobus, ma meno veloce dell'aereo.
examples.en: The train is more comfortable than the bus, but slower than the plane.

examples.it: In questa classe ci sono più italiani che stranieri.
examples.en: In this class there are more Italians than foreigners.

sections.tip: Quick test: if the two things being compared are on either side of a single adjective and are both nouns/pronouns, use *di*; if you could put *che* between two parallel items of the same type, use *che*.

sections.heading: Superlatives
sections.body: The relative superlative (*the most / the least*) is formed with the definite article plus *più/meno* and the adjective, with the group introduced by *di* (or *fra/tra*): *il ragazzo più alto della classe, la città meno cara d'Italia*. The article is not repeated when the adjective follows the noun (*il film più bello*, not *il film il più bello*). The absolute superlative (*very…*) is made by adding *-issimo/a/i/e* to the adjective stem (*bellissimo, facilissimo, elegantissima*); *-co/-go* adjectives keep the hard sound (*stanchissimo, larghissimo*). Alternatives are *molto/assai/estremamente* + adjective, prefixes like *stra-, arci-, super-* (*strapieno, arcinoto*), and repetition (*piano piano*).

examples.it: È la spiaggia più bella della Sardegna.
examples.en: It is the most beautiful beach in Sardinia.

examples.it: La pasta era buonissima e il conto bassissimo.
examples.en: The pasta was delicious and the bill very low.

sections.heading: Irregular comparatives: migliore, peggiore, maggiore, minore
sections.body: *Buono, cattivo, grande* and *piccolo* have regular forms (*più buono, più cattivo, più grande, più piccolo*) alongside Latin-derived irregular ones: *migliore* (better), *peggiore* (worse), *maggiore* (greater, elder, main), *minore* (smaller, younger, lesser). Their absolute superlatives are *ottimo, pessimo, massimo, minimo*, and their relative superlatives are *il migliore, il peggiore, il maggiore, il minore*. *Migliore* and *peggiore* are preferred for quality and abstract comparison; *più buono* often means literally tastier or kinder. *Maggiore/minore* are used for age among siblings (*il fratello maggiore*), importance (*la maggior parte*) and abstract size, while *più grande/più piccolo* is used for physical size. The adverbs work the same way: *bene → meglio, male → peggio* (never *più bene*).

examples.it: Questo ristorante è migliore di quello, ma il vino è pessimo.
examples.en: This restaurant is better than that one, but the wine is terrible.

examples.it: Mia sorella maggiore canta meglio di me.
examples.en: My elder sister sings better than I do.

sections.tip: *Migliore/peggiore* drop the final *-e* before a noun in fixed phrases: *il miglior amico, la peggior figura*. *Maggiore* likewise: *la maggior parte*.

title: The tense system
summary: A map of every Italian tense and mood: how each one is formed in one line, when it is used, and examples.

sections.heading: Overview: moods and tenses
sections.body: Italian verbs are organised into moods (*modi*) and, within each mood, tenses (*tempi*). The indicative states facts and has eight tenses: four simple (*presente, imperfetto, passato remoto, futuro semplice*) and four compound (*passato prossimo, trapassato prossimo, trapassato remoto, futuro anteriore*). The conditional has a present and a past, the subjunctive (*congiuntivo*) has four tenses, and the imperative has only a present. Every compound tense is built with the auxiliary *avere* or *essere* in the corresponding simple tense plus the past participle (*-ato, -uto, -ito*). Regular verbs fall into three conjugations by their infinitive ending: *-are* (*parlare*), *-ere* (*credere*), *-ire* (*dormire*, and the *-isc-* group like *finire*).
table: presente, imperfetto, passato remoto, futuro semplice
passato prossimo, trapassato prossimo, trapassato remoto, futuro anteriore

sections.heading: Presente
sections.body: Formation: stem + *-o, -i, -a/-e, -iamo, -ate/-ete/-ite, -ano/-ono*. The present covers what is happening now, general truths and habits, and, very commonly, the near future (*Domani parto*). Italian has no separate continuous form: *mangio* is both *I eat* and *I am eating*; *stare + gerundio* (*sto mangiando*) stresses that the action is in progress right now. The present with *da* + time expresses how long something has been going on: *Studio italiano da due anni* (I have been studying Italian for two years).

examples.it: Ogni mattina prendo il treno delle sette.
examples.en: Every morning I take the seven o'clock train.

examples.it: Abito a Torino da tre anni.
examples.en: I have been living in Turin for three years.

sections.heading: Passato prossimo and trapassato prossimo
sections.body: Passato prossimo: present of *avere* or *essere* + past participle (*ho parlato, sono andato*). It is the everyday past tense for completed actions and events, especially those with a link to the present or set in a defined time frame (*ieri, la settimana scorsa, due anni fa, già, mai*), and in the spoken language of most of Italy it has replaced the *passato remoto* even for distant events. With *essere* the participle agrees with the subject: *Maria è andata, i ragazzi sono partiti*. Trapassato prossimo: imperfect of *avere/essere* + participle (*avevo parlato, ero andato*); it is the past of the past, an action completed before another past action, typically after *quando, dopo che, appena, perché, già* (*Quando sono arrivato, il film era già cominciato*).

examples.it: Ieri sera abbiamo mangiato fuori.
examples.en: Last night we ate out.

examples.it: Laura è partita per Londra due giorni fa.
examples.en: Laura left for London two days ago.

examples.it: Non aveva mai visto il mare prima di quel viaggio.
examples.en: She had never seen the sea before that trip.

sections.heading: Imperfetto
sections.body: Formation: stem + *-avo/-evo/-ivo, -avi, -ava, -avamo, -avate, -avano* (the *-v-* is the signature); only *essere* is irregular (*ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano*), and a few verbs use an old stem (*fare → facevo, dire → dicevo, bere → bevevo, tradurre → traducevo*). It describes the past as ongoing or unfinished: background and description (weather, age, feelings, appearance), habits and repeated actions (*da bambino giocavo sempre fuori*), actions in progress when something else happened, and simultaneous actions. It is also used for politeness (*Volevo un caffè*) and in the *if*-clause of colloquial hypotheticals (*Se lo sapevo, venivo*).

examples.it: Quando ero piccolo, andavo al mare ogni estate.
examples.en: When I was little, I used to go to the seaside every summer.

examples.it: Pioveva e faceva freddo, così siamo rimasti a casa.
examples.en: It was raining and cold, so we stayed at home.

sections.heading: Passato remoto and trapassato remoto
sections.body: Passato remoto: stem + *-ai/-ei(-etti)/-ii, -asti/-esti/-isti, -ò/-é(-ette)/-ì, -ammo/-emmo/-immo, -aste/-este/-iste, -arono/-erono(-ettero)/-irono*; many *-ere* verbs are irregular in the *io, lui, loro* forms (*ebbi, dissi, feci, scrissi, vidi, venni, presi, seppi, volli, nacqui*) in a 1-3-3 pattern, with *tu, noi, voi* regular. It presents a completed action as detached from the present and is the tense of written narrative, history, biography and fairy tales; it is still current in spoken Southern Italian and Tuscan, while elsewhere speech uses the *passato prossimo*. You must recognise it to read literature and newspapers and to pass B2 and above. Trapassato remoto: *passato remoto* of *avere/essere* + participle (*ebbi parlato, fui andato*); it is literary and appears only after *quando, dopo che, (non) appena, finché* when the main verb is in the *passato remoto* (*Appena ebbe finito, tutti applaudirono*).

examples.it: Dante nacque a Firenze nel 1265 e morì a Ravenna nel 1321.
examples.en: Dante was born in Florence in 1265 and died in Ravenna in 1321.

examples.it: La principessa aprì la porta e vide un lupo.
examples.en: The princess opened the door and saw a wolf.

examples.it: Dopo che furono partiti, la casa rimase vuota.
examples.en: After they had left, the house remained empty.

sections.heading: Futuro semplice and futuro anteriore
sections.body: Futuro semplice: infinitive minus the final *-e* + *-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno*; *-are* verbs change *a* to *e* (*parlerò*), and some verbs contract the stem (*avrò, andrò, saprò, vedrò, vivrò, potrò, dovrò, verrò, vorrò, rimarrò, berrò, terrò, sarò*), while *fare, dare, stare* keep their *a* (*farò, darò, starò*). It expresses future actions, promises and predictions, and, very often, conjecture about the present (*Sarà a casa* = he is probably at home; *Che ore saranno?*). Futuro anteriore: future of *avere/essere* + participle (*avrò parlato, sarò andato*); it marks an action that will be completed before another future action (*Quando avrò finito, ti chiamerò*) and conjecture about the past (*Avrà perso il treno* = he must have missed the train).

examples.it: L'anno prossimo andremo in Giappone.
examples.en: Next year we will go to Japan.

examples.it: Quando avrai letto il libro, me lo presterai?
examples.en: When you have read the book, will you lend it to me?

examples.it: Non risponde: sarà uscito.
examples.en: He's not answering: he must have gone out.

sections.tip: After *quando, appena, se* Italian uses the future where English uses the present: *Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò*.

sections.heading: Condizionale presente and passato
sections.body: Condizionale presente: same stem as the future + *-ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero* (*parlerei, avrei, sarei, andrei, vorrei*). It expresses what would happen under a condition, polite requests and wishes (*Vorrei un caffè; Potresti aiutarmi?*), advice (*Dovresti riposare*), and unconfirmed reports (*Il ministro sarebbe pronto a dimettersi*). Condizionale passato: conditional of *avere/essere* + participle (*avrei parlato, sarei andato*); it expresses what would have happened (*Sarei venuto, ma ero malato*), unconfirmed past reports, and, unlike English, the future in the past: *Ha detto che sarebbe arrivato alle otto* (he said he would arrive at eight).

examples.it: Mi piacerebbe vivere al mare.
examples.en: I would like to live by the sea.

examples.it: Avrei comprato la casa, ma costava troppo.
examples.en: I would have bought the house, but it cost too much.

examples.it: Mi ha promesso che mi avrebbe scritto.
examples.en: She promised me she would write to me.

sections.tip: Distinguish *parleremo* (future, one m) from *parleremmo* (conditional, double m).

sections.heading: Congiuntivo: presente, passato, imperfetto, trapassato
sections.body: Congiuntivo presente: stem + *-i, -i, -i, -iamo, -iate, -ino* for *-are* verbs and *-a, -a, -a, -iamo, -iate, -ano* for *-ere/-ire* verbs (*creda, dorma, finisca*), with irregulars such as *sia, abbia, vada, faccia, dica, possa, voglia, debba, sappia, stia, dia, venga, esca*; the *passato* is *abbia/sia* + participle. Congiuntivo imperfetto: stem + *-assi/-essi/-issi, -assi/-essi/-issi, -asse/-esse/-isse, -assimo/-essimo/-issimo, -aste/-este/-iste, -assero/-essero/-issero* (irregular only *fossi, dessi, stessi* and old-stem *facessi, dicessi, bevessi, traducessi*); the *trapassato* is *avessi/fossi* + participle. The subjunctive is required in subordinate clauses after verbs of opinion, doubt, wish, emotion and necessity (*penso che, credo che, voglio che, spero che, è necessario che, mi dispiace che*), after conjunctions like *benché, sebbene, affinché, purché, prima che, a meno che, senza che*, after indefinites (*chiunque, qualunque*) and in relative clauses after a superlative or *unico* (*È il film più bello che abbia visto*). Sequence of tenses: with a present or future main verb use *presente* (same time or later) or *passato* (earlier): *Penso che abbia ragione; Spero che siate arrivati bene*; with a past or conditional main verb use *imperfetto* (same time or later) or *trapassato* (earlier): *Pensavo che fosse stanco; Non sapevo che avesse già mangiato; Vorrei che tu venissi*. The imperfect and *trapassato* also build hypotheticals (*Se avessi tempo, viaggerei; Se avessi avuto tempo, avrei viaggiato*) and follow *come se* and *magari* (*Parla come se fosse un esperto; Magari fosse vero!*). Because the three singular forms are identical, the subject pronoun is often stated.

examples.it: Penso che Luca abbia ragione.
examples.en: I think Luca is right.

examples.it: Credevo che tu fossi a Roma.
examples.en: I thought you were in Rome.

examples.it: Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto prima.
examples.en: If I had known, I would have come earlier.

sections.tip: No subjunctive after verbs of certainty (*so che, è chiaro che, sono sicuro che*) or when both clauses share a subject: *Penso di avere ragione*, not *penso che io abbia*.

sections.heading: Imperativo
sections.body: Formation: *tu* uses the present indicative ending except for *-are* verbs, which take *-a* (*parla! credi! dormi! finisci!*); *noi* and *voi* are identical to the present indicative (*parliamo! parlate!*); the formal *Lei* and *Loro* use the present subjunctive (*parli! parlino!*). The negative *tu* imperative is *non* + infinitive (*Non parlare!*); the other persons simply add *non*. Irregular *tu* forms include *sii, abbi, sappi, va'/vai, fa'/fai, da'/dai, sta'/stai, di'*. The imperative gives orders, instructions, advice and invitations, and it is softened with *pure, per favore* or *un attimo*.

examples.it: Prendi l'ombrello, non dimenticarlo!
examples.en: Take the umbrella, don't forget it!

examples.it: Signora, si accomodi e aspetti un attimo.
examples.en: Madam, take a seat and wait a moment.

title: Passato prossimo vs imperfetto
summary: When a past action is a completed event (passato prossimo) and when it is ongoing, habitual or background (imperfetto), how the two work together in a story, and how stare + gerundio fits in.

sections.heading: The core contrast
sections.body: Both tenses talk about the past, but they look at it differently. The *passato prossimo* presents an action as a completed event with a beginning and an end, a point on the timeline: *Ho mangiato una pizza*. The *imperfetto* presents an action as a state or a process seen from the inside, without focusing on its start or finish: *Mangiavo una pizza (quando…)*. The choice is not about how long ago something happened but about whether you are reporting an event or describing a situation.
table: ongoing situation, no end in view
single action or a counted series (tre volte)
Ieri lavoravo quando mi hai chiamato.

examples.it: Ho vissuto a Milano per cinque anni.
examples.en: I lived in Milan for five years (completed period).

examples.it: Vivevo a Milano quando ho conosciuto Sara.
examples.en: I was living in Milan when I met Sara.

sections.heading: What the imperfetto is for
sections.body: Use the *imperfetto* to describe people, places, weather and feelings in the past (*Era alto, aveva gli occhi verdi; Faceva caldo; Ero stanco*), to give age and clock time (*Avevo dieci anni; Erano le tre*), for habits and repeated actions (*Ogni estate andavamo in montagna; La domenica mangiavamo dalla nonna*), for two actions going on at the same time (*Mentre lui cucinava, io leggevo*), for mental states and intentions (*Pensavo che fosse vero; Volevo dirtelo*), and for an action in progress interrupted by another. Verbs of state and perception (*essere, avere, sapere, conoscere, volere, sembrare, stare*) are very often in the *imperfetto* because they naturally describe situations rather than events.

examples.it: Da bambina avevo i capelli lunghi e portavo sempre gli occhiali.
examples.en: As a child I had long hair and always wore glasses.

examples.it: Era mezzanotte, la strada era deserta e nevicava.
examples.en: It was midnight, the street was deserted and it was snowing.

examples.it: Mentre aspettavo l'autobus, ascoltavo la musica.
examples.en: While I was waiting for the bus, I was listening to music.

sections.heading: What the passato prossimo is for
sections.body: Use the *passato prossimo* for single completed actions (*Ho comprato il pane*), for a sequence of events one after the other (*Mi sono alzato, ho fatto colazione e sono uscito*), for actions that happened a specific number of times (*Sono andato in Sicilia tre volte*), for an action with a stated, closed duration (*Ha lavorato lì per due anni*), and for a sudden change of state or feeling (*Ho avuto paura; Ha capito tutto*). Even long-lasting situations take the *passato prossimo* if they are presented as finished blocks: *Sono stato malato per un mese*.

examples.it: Stamattina mi sono svegliato tardi, ho perso il treno e sono arrivato in ritardo.
examples.en: This morning I woke up late, missed the train and arrived late.

examples.it: Abbiamo abitato a Bologna dal 2010 al 2015.
examples.en: We lived in Bologna from 2010 to 2015.

examples.it: Quando ho visto il conto, ho avuto un colpo.
examples.en: When I saw the bill, I got a shock.

sections.heading: Signal words
sections.body: Time expressions are strong clues but not laws: what matters is whether the action is presented as an event or as a situation. Words that count or bound an action point to the *passato prossimo*; words that express repetition, duration without limits or simultaneity point to the *imperfetto*. Note that *sempre* and *mai* work with both: *Ha sempre lavorato molto* (over a whole finished period) versus *Lavorava sempre fino a tardi* (habit).

examples.it: Di solito prendevo l'autobus, ma ieri ho preso un taxi.
examples.en: I usually took the bus, but yesterday I took a taxi.

examples.it: All'improvviso la luce è andata via.
examples.en: Suddenly the power went out.

sections.heading: The two tenses together in narration
sections.body: A story in Italian alternates the two tenses. The *imperfetto* paints the background, what was going on, how things looked and felt; the *passato prossimo* supplies the events that happen against that background and push the story forward. The classic pattern is an action in progress (*imperfetto*) interrupted by a sudden event (*passato prossimo*), typically with *mentre* or *quando*: *Mentre dormivo, è suonato il telefono; Guardavo la TV quando è arrivato Marco*. When *quando* introduces two events in sequence, both go in the *passato prossimo*: *Quando è arrivato Marco, abbiamo cenato*.
table: Era una bella giornata e c'era molta gente in spiaggia.
A un certo punto un bambino ha gridato.
Camminavo per il centro e pensavo ai fatti miei,
quando ho incontrato un vecchio compagno di scuola.
così ho ordinato solo un caffè.

examples.it: Ieri sera pioveva, non avevo voglia di uscire, quindi ho ordinato una pizza e ho guardato un film.
examples.en: Last night it was raining, I didn't feel like going out, so I ordered a pizza and watched a film.

examples.it: Mentre facevo la doccia, qualcuno ha bussato alla porta.
examples.en: While I was having a shower, someone knocked at the door.

sections.tip: Ask two questions: *What happened?* (event → passato prossimo) and *What was it like / what was going on?* (situation → imperfetto).

sections.heading: Verbs that change meaning: sapere, conoscere, potere, volere, dovere
sections.body: With verbs of knowledge and modality the tense choice changes the English translation. *Sapevo* means *I knew*, while *ho saputo* means *I found out*. *Conoscevo* is *I knew (someone)*, *ho conosciuto* is *I met (for the first time)*. *Volevo* is *I wanted (to)*, *ho voluto* is *I insisted on / decided to*; *non ho voluto* is *I refused*. *Potevo* is *I was able to (in general)*, *ho potuto* is *I managed to (on that occasion)*. *Dovevo* is *I was supposed to* (with no guarantee I did), *ho dovuto* is *I had to (and did)*.

examples.it: Non sapevo che fossi sposato: l'ho saputo solo ieri.
examples.en: I didn't know you were married: I only found out yesterday.

examples.it: Volevo chiamarti, ma non ho potuto.
examples.en: I wanted to call you, but I couldn't.

sections.heading: Stare + gerundio: the progressive
sections.body: *Stare* + gerund (*-ando* for *-are* verbs, *-endo* for *-ere/-ire*: *parlando, leggendo, dormendo*; irregular *facendo, dicendo, bevendo, traducendo, ponendo*) highlights that an action is in progress at a precise moment. In the present, *sto mangiando* is a more emphatic *mangio*; in the past, *stavo mangiando* is a more emphatic *mangiavo* and is used only in the *imperfetto* form, never with the *passato prossimo*. It is the natural choice for the interrupted-action pattern: *Stavo uscendo quando è squillato il telefono*. It cannot express habits, states or the future, so *Sto abitando a Roma* is wrong for *I live in Rome*, and *sto andando* cannot mean *I am going (tomorrow)*.

examples.it: Cosa stai facendo? Sto cucinando.
examples.en: What are you doing? I'm cooking.

examples.it: I bambini stavano giocando in giardino quando ha cominciato a piovere.
examples.en: The children were playing in the garden when it started to rain.

sections.tip: Pronouns can go before *stare* or attach to the gerund: *lo sto leggendo* or *sto leggendolo*.

title: Essere or avere?
summary: Which auxiliary each verb takes in compound tenses, how the participle agrees, what happens with modal verbs, and the verbs that take both.

sections.heading: Transitive verbs take avere
sections.body: Every compound tense (*passato prossimo, trapassato, futuro anteriore, condizionale passato, congiuntivo passato…*) is built with *avere* or *essere* plus the past participle. The first and biggest rule is that a verb used transitively, that is with a direct object, always takes *avere*: *Ho mangiato la pasta; Abbiamo visto un film; Hai letto il giornale?*. This holds even when the object is left unsaid (*Ho già mangiato*). The participle after *avere* normally stays in the masculine singular form.

examples.it: Ho comprato due biglietti per il concerto.
examples.en: I bought two tickets for the concert.

examples.it: Hanno finito il lavoro in tempo.
examples.en: They finished the work on time.

sections.tip: Test: can you ask *chi? / che cosa?* after the verb and get a direct object? Then *avere*.

sections.heading: Intransitives of motion, change and state take essere
sections.body: Intransitive verbs that express movement from one place to another, a change of state, or staying in a state take *essere*: *andare, venire, arrivare, partire, entrare, uscire, tornare, salire, scendere, cadere, nascere, morire, diventare, crescere, invecchiare, guarire, restare, rimanere, stare, essere* itself. Impersonal verbs and verbs of happening also take *essere* (*succedere, accadere, capitare, bastare, servire, sembrare, costare, valere, piacere, mancare, dispiacere*), as do weather verbs (*è piovuto* or *ha piovuto*, both accepted). With *essere* the participle agrees with the subject in gender and number.

examples.it: Maria è uscita alle otto ed è tornata a mezzanotte.
examples.en: Maria went out at eight and came back at midnight.

examples.it: I prezzi sono aumentati e la qualità è peggiorata.
examples.en: Prices have gone up and quality has got worse.

sections.heading: Intransitives that still take avere
sections.body: Many intransitive verbs describe an activity rather than a movement or change, and these take *avere*: *dormire, camminare, viaggiare, lavorare, ridere, piangere, parlare, telefonare, rispondere, sorridere, sciare, nuotare, passeggiare, giocare, ballare, cenare, pranzare, abitare, funzionare, tossire, starnutire*. The distinction is between moving somewhere (*essere*) and the activity of moving (*avere*): *Sono andato a piedi* but *Ho camminato per due ore*. Verbs of sound and bodily activity (*dormire, russare, ridere, tossire*) are always *avere*.

examples.it: Ho dormito dieci ore e ho camminato tutto il giorno.
examples.en: I slept ten hours and walked all day.

examples.it: Le ho telefonato ieri, ma non ha risposto.
examples.en: I phoned her yesterday, but she didn't answer.

sections.heading: Reflexive, pronominal and impersonal si take essere
sections.body: All verbs used with a reflexive or pronominal pronoun (*mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si*) take *essere*, whatever their meaning: *mi sono alzato, si è lavata, ci siamo divertiti, si sono incontrati, se n'è andato*. The participle agrees with the subject: *Anna si è svegliata; i ragazzi si sono vestiti*. The impersonal or passive *si* also takes *essere*: *Si è mangiato bene; Si sono vendute molte case*, and with the impersonal *si* the participle of a normally-*avere* verb stays masculine singular while that of an *essere* verb goes plural (*Si è andati al mare*). Note that *lavarsi le mani* keeps *essere* even though there is a direct object: *Mi sono lavato le mani*.

examples.it: Ci siamo svegliati tardi e ci siamo vestiti in fretta.
examples.en: We woke up late and got dressed in a hurry.

examples.it: Si è parlato molto di questo problema.
examples.en: There has been a lot of talk about this problem.

sections.heading: Participle agreement
sections.body: With *essere* the participle always agrees with the subject: *è andato / andata / andati / andate*. With *avere* the participle agrees with a direct object only when that object comes before the verb as a pronoun; agreement is compulsory with *lo, la, li, le* and with *ne* (*L'ho vista; Li ho comprati; Le ho mangiate; Ne ho presi due*), and optional with *mi, ti, ci, vi* used as direct objects (*Ci hanno visti* or *visto*). Before *ho/ha/hai/hanno*, *lo* and *la* elide to *l'* (*l'ho visto, l'ho vista*), while *li* and *le* never elide. With reflexive verbs and a direct object pronoun, the participle agrees with the object rather than the subject: *Mi sono lavato le mani → Me le sono lavate*.
